title: Learning the language of machine learning

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student and her advisor discuss how to make an AI model's decision-making more transparent.

script.en: Professor, I've been working on the deep learning model for medical image classification, and it performs well on the test set, but I'm worried that we can't really explain why it makes certain predictions.
That's a common concern, especially in high-stakes domains. Have you looked into the interpretability techniques we discussed last semester?
I have, but most of them seem to focus on visualizing attention maps. They tell us where the model is looking, not why it reaches a particular conclusion.
Right. Visualization is a start, but it doesn't give you a verbal explanation. What if we trained the model to generate natural language descriptions of its own reasoning process?
You mean like a self-explanation? I've read a couple of papers on that, but the explanations often sound plausible yet are not faithful to the actual computation.

Exactly. Faithfulness is the key challenge. If the explanation is just another learned pattern that happens to correlate with the output, it's not trustworthy. We need to design training objectives that reward accurate self-reporting.
That sounds promising, but how do we evaluate whether an explanation is faithful? We can't read the model's mind.

We can run counterfactual tests. For instance, if the model says it relies on a particular feature, we can remove that feature and see if the prediction changes accordingly. If it doesn't, the explanation is likely unfaithful.
That makes sense. So the idea is to use behavioral tests to validate the model's own descriptions.
Precisely. And that's what I'd like you to explore for your thesis project. Start by reviewing the recent work on self-explanatory models, and then we can design a set of counterfactual experiments.
I'll do that. I'm excited about this direction—it feels like we're teaching the model to communicate, not just to predict.
That's the spirit. Let's meet next week to discuss your experimental design.

script.en: In recent years, artificial intelligence has moved rapidly from research laboratories into everyday applications, ranging from recommendation systems that shape what we read and watch to medical diagnosis tools that help doctors in clinical decision-making. As these systems become increasingly powerful and pervasive, however, a critical question arises: can we trust them to explain their own decisions in ways that ordinary users can understand? A team of researchers at a major university has been tackling this challenge by developing what they call "self-explanatory" AI models. Rather than relying on external tools to interpret a model's behavior after the fact, the team trains the model itself to generate accurate natural language descriptions of its internal reasoning. The approach is grounded in the belief that a model can be taught to communicate what it has learned from data in a way that humans can readily understand. The researchers argue that this is especially important in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or finance, where a wrong decision can have serious consequences for people and institutions alike. To ensure that the explanations are trustworthy, the team uses counterfactual testing: they modify the input to see whether the model's explanation correctly predicts how its output will change. If the explanation fails to match the actual behavior, it is considered unfaithful and the model is retrained. Early results are promising, but the researchers caution that the work is still in its infancy. They note that generating faithful explanations is computationally demanding and that current models sometimes produce plausible but misleading descriptions. but, they believe that teaching machines to talk about themselves is a crucial step toward building AI systems that humans can genuinely collaborate with and trust.

sections.title: Teaching Machines to Explain Themselves
sections.passage: When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers want to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable AI models to communicate accurately about what they learned from training data, in language humans can understand. “Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). By studying how machines come to understand language, Andreas and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators. They develop methods to make the training process more natural and efficient, so AI models learn in a way that is more like human learning. “We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says. Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on. That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming. “I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says. Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text. “I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls. Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems. Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning. Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data.
